content: Cryoprecipitate is a blood product derived from plasma. Each 15 mL unit of cryoprecipitate contains approximately 100 units of factor VIII, 250 mg of fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibronectin. According to established standards, each bag of cryoprecipitate must contain a minimum of 150 mg of fibrinogen, although most bags typically contain around 250 mg, which is the value commonly used in clinical calculations. Additionally, each bag must contain at least 80 international units (IU) of factor VIII. The clinical indications for administering cryoprecipitate include the following: Hemophilia: Cryoprecipitate is used as an emergency backup treatment when specific factor concentrates are unavailable. Von Willebrand’s disease: It can be used in certain cases to manage this condition. Hypofibrinogenaemia: This refers to low fibrinogen levels, which can occur in scenarios such as massive transfusions. Bleeding due to excessive anticoagulation: While plasma contains most coagulation factors and is generally a better option for rapidly reversing anticoagulation, cryoprecipitate may be used in specific situations. Massive hemorrhage: In such cases, red blood cells (RBCs) and volume expanders are typically more effective choices for managing the condition.
